speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Monday last the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) alleged on a question of privilege that I had misled the house. I now rise on a question of privilege to correct him. The hon. member was dealing with the question of the buying prices established for grain in western Canada, and I quote his words from page 4397 of Hansard, as follows:
The second question had to do with the exact buying prices, to which the minister replied that he did not have the figures in mind at that time. I had asked whether the figures were the same as the previous year. There are a great many grades and if there had been changes I would not and did not expect the minister to know, but on checking the figures set forth in the order in council and the prices for the grades in the previous year I can find no change in the grades set forth. I find that they are exactly the same.
I feel that the answer was misleading, though I do not suggest deliberately so.
I must say that was extremely charitable of the hon. member, but the facts are otherwise. He was referring to the Canada Gazette of August 27, 1958 and I presume compared the figures in that publication with the figures in the Canada Gazette of August 27, 1957, the publication for the previous year. I draw the attention of the house to the following facts. No. 1 Canada western amber durum is shown at a price of $1.50 in 1957 and $1.40 for 1958. No. 2 Canada western amber durum was $1.47 for last year and is $1.36 now. The No. 3 grade was $1.40 last year and is $1.30 now. In all, seven grades show substantial changes.
The hon. member for Assiniboia examined the Gazettes according to his own admission, yet he informed the house on Monday that there had been no changes. I make no comment as to whether or not the hon. member was deliberately misleading the house.

subtopic: MR. CHURCHILL    REPLY TO STATEMENT BY HON. MEMBER FOR ASSINIBOIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if I may reply, also on a question of privilege, I frankly admit that I did not check the amber durum prices. I checked wheat as wheat is commonly known in the trade. Durum wheat is known as amber durum, as
the minister has referred to it. Wheat is known as bread wheat. I checked wheat, oats and barley, and there was no change. But the first part of my statement has not been alluded to by the minister, namely that it was his order in council that recommended these prices, and though the question was asked two days later apparently the minister did not know it had taken place.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: MR. CHURCHILL    REPLY TO STATEMENT BY HON. MEMBER FOR ASSINIBOIA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is once again attempting to mislead the house. I answered the first part of his question on Monday. subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT RESPECTING VISIT OF HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN AND PRINCE PHILIP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the house will be pleased to know that Her Majesty the Queen has now graciously agreed that her visit to Canada next year with Prince Philip will take place approximately from the middle of June to the end of July, and that the tour will extend to all parts of our country.
While announcing the timing and the general duration of Her Majesty's tour, it is not possible as yet, of course, to be more specific as to the dates or as to the special items and cities and towns to be included in the program. A number of suggestions have been received which will be considered by a special committee appointed for this purpose, and further announcements will be made later when Her Majesty has considered the recommendations of that committee for the general program of her tour.
Canadians in all parts of Canada I am sure will welcome Her Majesty's decision to spend some weeks with us and to travel extensively across the country. When she inaugurates

Questions
the St. Lawrence seaway Her Majesty will associate herself with the completion of a project which is bound to have profound significance in our national development. It will be a source of satisfaction to all Canadians that Her Majesty, in opening a new chapter in our history, will thus exemplify in vivid fashion a characteristic of our constitution involving the close relationship between the Queen and her people of Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of ihe Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT RESPECTING VISIT OF HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN AND PRINCE PHILIP
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we on this side will share in the pleasure of all Canadians in the announcement the Prime Minister has just made that next summer the Queen is to visit her realm of Canada. That pleasure will be increased by the knowledge that she is to be accompanied by her husband, Prince Philip. It is also increased by the Prime Minister's announcement that she will be here not merely to open this great national and international undertaking, the St. Lawrence seaway, but that she will also have a chance to visit all parts of our country. She will, I know, receive the warm and enthusiastic welcome that she and her husband have received on previous visits to this country. Her visit will give us an additional opportunity to show our loyalty to the crown as a cornerstone of our democratic institutions.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: URANIUM CITY, SASK.    CONSTRUCTION AND ROUTE OF ACCESS ROAD
speechtext:
I do not want to delay the committee while waiting for a document, Mr. Chairman. I thought I should like to make a short statement under three headings, namely what the federal government is doing with regard to research; some comments with regard to the laboratories of the national research council; then the problem of university support, concluding with mention of some highlights in the estimates themselves.
The national research council has three essential functions, namely the promotion and co-ordination of scientific research in Canada, the operation of laboratories, and the financial support of university research in science. The research carried on by the agencies of the Canadian government is of high quality, the facilities and conditions of work are good, and funds in considerable quantity are being provided for that purpose. It is estimated that when you consider all the money being expended for the purpose of research under federal government auspices it is approaching $140 million, which is a considerable sum for a country the size of Canada.
Sometimes expenditures of this nature are compared with those of other countries, and we naturally look to the United States to see what that country is doing along that line. The comparisons are of necessity rather rough, since accounting systems and definitions vary; but dealing with the subject of research for civilian purposes, I may say that Canada's showing is very good and shows, on a per capita basis, a figure slightly above that of the United States. But then when you add all the money that is being spent on research, adding military expenditures in the United States along with their civil expenditures for research you find, of course, that they vastly exceed those of Canada. The emphasis that is placed on military research in other countries such as Russia and the United Kingdom indicates also that they have very high expenditures for this purpose. Nevertheless, on the civilian side Canada's position is good, and it is expected that the continuing expansion of technology would require a continued expansion in government civilian research.
On the question of the laboratories, the laboratories of the national research council carry out fundamental and applied research in science and engineering which is of national importance and which is not being done elsewhere. The work is organized in eight scientific divisions in Ottawa and two regional laboratories at Halifax and Saskatoon. The laboratories have undergone a steady growth since 1939, when the staff was only about 300 until today, when in spite of having split off defence research and atomic energy the staff numbers 2353.

During this expansion every effort has been made to maintain a steady and effective expansion of the laboratories as manpower considerations permitted. This steady increase is being continued. On June 30, 1957, the staff numbered 2260, on August 11, 1958 it numbered 2353, and the estimates allow for a further expansion to 2422 by the end of the fiscal year. Further, this year's expansion is being concentrated on scientific staff, who number at present 647 and will be recruited, it is hoped, to 700 by the end of the fiscal year. There is nothing spectacular in the estimates for the laboratories, but they permit a steady and efficient expansion as in the past.
On the subject of university support, which is of general interest, recent events have emphasized the importance of an extended effort among the western countries in basic research in science and medicine. The universities are the major source of such research and are also the sole source of trained personnel for research of all kinds. In Canada the main financial support for university scientific research, as distinct from teaching, has for 40 years been the national research council. Sizeable contributions are made for special purposes by other government agencies, but all of these are considerably smaller than the support from the council itself.
I should not like to give the impression that the national research council is the only one which has done research in Canada, because the pioneering work in research was commenced by agriculture and mining in days gone by. Since that time the national research council and other government agencies have entered the field. While as I have said, sizeable contributions are made for special purposes by other government agencies, all of these are considerably smaller than the support from the council. Support from private agencies is smaller still. In view of the magnitude of the research council support and its 40 years of operation it can be claimed with considerable justification that the present status of Canadian science is largely due to financial support from the national research council.
The expansion of the universities, together with the desirability of scientific expansion in the western world, however, has made the financial problems of university scientific research very difficult. Recognizing this, the government decided to increase national research council support to universities by 70 per cent in the present estimates. This increase of $2J million is by far the largest increase which has ever been made in the

I take it from the minister's statement-and I hope he will correct me if I am not accurate-that the national research council is continuing the policy of the previous government. I also take it from his remarks that he shares the view concerning the work of the council that was expressed in the committee in 1956 when the estimates were last before it, an occasion when high praise of the council was expressed. He will recall that on that occasion two hon. gentlemen in the then opposition, the present Minister of Public Works and the present Minister of Veterans Affairs, spoke in praise of the work of the research council as it was conducted under the previous government. I take it that he shares that view and that there is no change in policy with respect to the research council.
I had the honour of heading the committees that looked into the work and activities of the research council since the end of the war and also the committees dealing with the operations of the atomic energy control board since that time. I must say I hold the view that the activities conducted by the government through the national research council were such as to commend themselves to hon. members on all sides of the house.
I must frankly admit I have always had a particularly favourable impression of the way they conducted their work in conjunction with the universities. Instead of drawing off manpower from the universities and in that way damaging them, they have sought to aid the work of the universities and have carried out that policy in different ways, through grants in aid of scholarships and fellowships. I believe the outstanding work done in the last number of years in that field has not had sufficient public acknowledgment or sufficient appreciation by hon. members, if I may speak for my colleagues in that respect.
At this stage of the session I do not have any further specific questions to ask about the estimates of the national research council.
I merely want to encourage the minister to continue the activity of this body in the way in which it has been conducted in the past, and to seek to support and expand it as the development of the country goes on.

speechtext:
Thank you very much. I have a rather comprehensive statement to make on this topic, which is of major importance nowadays. I hope hon. members of the committee will bear with me for the next 15 minutes as I review the activities of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited and indicate the objectives of that organization. The activities of that body may be considered in four general categories: (a) fundamental research (b) applied research (c) production and marketing of radioactive isotopes and (d) power reactor projects. I discussed the nature and objectives of these categories in my statement to parliament on February 1 last, and I would now like to bring that statement up to date and give a broad summary of each of these four categories of activities, dealing first with fundamental research.
The great developments in atomic energy during and since the war were based on a working capital of fundamental scientific knowledge built up earlier and especially during the 1930's. Our debt to Ernest Rutherford and to the scientists of several nations who followed him in exploring the physics of the atomic nucleus is one which can never be overemphasized. The present worldwide development of atomic energy is still drawing on that original capital of fundamental knowledge, and it is incumbent upon us to try to add to it to the extent that our resources permit.
Chalk River has lived up to its obligations in this regard. From the early days Canadian fundamental research has been held in high international esteem. At present Chalk River is pioneering in a number of new fields, and as an example I would mention the theoretical studies by one of the Chalk River physicists on the thermonuclear reactions that occur in stars. This work, which has attracted considerable attention, is leading to a better understanding of nuclear processes and has been made possible through the use of the electronic computer installed at Chalk River in 1956.
In the early days it was often possible to carry out fundamental nuclear research with very simple equipment. However, as the science has steadily become more complex it has been necessary to turn to increasingly powerful tools. The NRX reactor and a Van de Graaf machine have been the main tools

Supply-Trade and Commerce of fundamental research at Chalk River over the past decade. To ensure continued progress it has been necessary to add new equipment. A very precise beta-ray spectrometer has recently been brought into operation; a new high energy Van de Graaf is under construction, as well as special facilities for the study of the changes occurring in metals during irradiation.
But the most important of the new tools is the NRU reactor, which makes possible many experiments which hitherto could not be performed. In many of its facilities NRU is unequalled by any other reactor in the world and provides unique opportunities to Canadian fundamental research.
Fundamental research also has other uses. It is an extremely effective training ground for young men who in later years will turn to applied research and the exploitation of scientific knowledge. The applied research program at Chalk River has to a large extent depended on the contributions of men who began their careers in fundamental research. Another bypath of a healthy fundamental research program is that it tends to leaven the whole of the activities of an establishment like that at Chalk River. Daily contact with colleagues engaged in truly creative work acts as a stimulant to those involved in the applied research and development programs and contributes markedly to the rate of progress achieved. Canada's position as one of the leading atomic powers will be maintained only so long as we are prepared to devote some of our resources to the kind of research that lays the foundations on which all practical developments are based.
Applied research at Chalk River is mainly concerned with the translation of fundamental knowledge into sound reactor technology. Nuclear engineering brings together a wide variety of different disciplines. Complex electronic instruments are needed; the chemical and corrosive properties of the various liquids in a reactor system must be carefully controlled; radiation hazards must be thoroughly understood and the engineering design adjusted to minimize them; new fields in structural and mechanical engineering are opened up by the employment of novel materials; for example the metal zirconium, about which very little was known 10 years ago.
While all these problems are receiving attention in the applied research program at Chalk River, the largest effort is devoted to two problems that will have a decisive effect on our efforts to achieve economic nuclear power. The first of these is the improvement of uranium fuel elements, the 

second is the design of more efficient arrangements for the reactor core.
The heat contained in a ton of natural uranium is equivalent to the heat contained in 2,700,000 tons of coal. It is this basic fact which has given to atomic energy its great significance as a new source of fuel for power plants. But how much of the heat contained in a ton of uranium fuel can one release and use? Obviously the more use one can obtain the more efficient the reactor will be and the more likely it is that the electricity produced will be economic. Therefore the design, fabrication and testing of uranium fuel systems is an essential part of the applied research program.
The testing of such systems is carried out in the NRX and NRU reactors, where it is possible to simulate the conditions that will prevail in a nuclear power station. The testing is done in equipment known as "loops" which pass through the heart of the reactor. There are six such loops working continuously in NRX, which in effect are six separate reactors using different materials of construction, different coolants and different fuels operating under a variety of conditions. New loops in NRU will permit further engineering studies of various power reactor systems, including those cooled by gas as well as those cooled by liquids. New metallurgical laboratories under construction will be important for the examination of experimental fuel elements after removal from the loops as well as for fundamental research. Many of the studies in loops are carried out in co-operation with the United States atomic energy commission and the United Kingdom atomic energy authority.
The efficiency of a reactor depends to a large degree on the design of its core. The design of a reactor core requires careful calculation and experiment, since its behaviour depends critically on the size, shape and arrangement of the fuel and other components that are contained in it. Reactor cores are studied in the ZEEP reactor. The letters stand for zero energy experimental pile, which first came into operation in 1945, when it was one of the first reactors in the world. ZEEP was used to work out the best arrangement for the core of NRX, and when NRU was designed ZEEP was used to find the best arrangement for that reactor, too. It has recently been remodelled and is now being used to work out arrangements for our proposed power reactors.
However, as these reactors will be considerably larger than ZEEP itself, only part of a core can be studied at one time. It is therefore proposed to build a new, large

ZEEP so the complete core of a power reactor can be specified precisely and costly margins need not be left to cover unknown factors.
Another new reactor, the PTR, the pool test reactor, is in use for related experiments. In these one determines just how much a piece of fuel will contribute to the reaction. This reactor is unique in that it was designed especially for the purpose and can measure pieces of fuel at intervals during their service in other reactors. With ZEEP, the new large ZEEP and PTR, Chalk River will be well equipped to obtain the precise information required to design cores for future economic power reactors.
Applied search in the use of plutonium as a reactor fuel has been pursued to the point where Canada has a leading position in this field. In addition, applied research at Chalk River indicates what appear to be economic methods of disposing of radioactive wastes.
For many years considerations of security kept secret much of the fundamental and virtually all of the applied research at Chalk River. Fortunately in recent years it has become possible to remove these restrictions, and the work of the research scientists is now freely published and discussed. Much of it has recently been reviewed and has been recorded for presentation at the second conference on the peaceful uses of atomic energy organized under the United Nations at Geneva, which I believe is now in progress.
On the subject of production and marketing of radioactive isotopes, the commercial products division of AECL, was established to develop markets for radioisotopes produced in the Chalk River reactors. This work involves processing and selling, but in addition a considerable amount of applied development and design of accessory equipment must be done in order to develop uses and maintain markets. The already wide application of isotopes in many branches of industry, agriculture, research and medicine is expanding and will no doubt continue to expand. The volume of business of this division has steadily increased to where it is now levelling out at about $2,500,000 per year. There has been a very marked increase in the curie quantities of radioactive material produced; for example, 94,000 curies were shipped in 1956 and 196,000 curies in 1957.
The principal source of revenue continues to be cobalt 60 and cobalt 60 beam therapy machines. Four models of these machines are available on a production basis, and one other is ready for production. About 115 machines have been installed in 20 countries. Since about 85 per cent of the business is export, and in a highly competitive market, world
Supply-Trade and Commerce trade conditions and the premium value of the Canadian dollar are having their effect in limiting the volume of sales.
This division operates as a separate accounting unit and tries to break even on its operations. It continues to have a relatively large program of development, with special emphasis on the use of radioisotopes. From 15 to 20 per cent of total revenues are invested in development work, which is considerably more than is normal in a purely commercial operation. In spite of this the cumulative loss of the division since 1952 has been held to $54,000.
I now deal with power reactor projects. This is a field in which the experience with atomic energy leads to its practical application in the development of power. It has been established for many years that electric power can be produced from a nuclear plant, but it is also recognized in all nuclear power programs that the economics of nuclear power can only be demonstrated by designing, engineering, constructing and operating nuclear power stations. It is because of this fact that it has become the practice to refer to the first round of power reactors now in operation or under construction as demonstration power reactors. Examples are the Calder Hall station in the United Kingdom, the PWR station in the United States, the G-2 and G-3 stations in France and our own NPD reactor in Canada.
While the fuel costs in a nuclear power station will be lower than the fuel costs in conventional thermal stations, the capital cost of nuclear power stations will be higher. The capital cost of the first round of demonstration power reactors will range fom $600 per kilowatt to $1,000 per kilowatt. This cost must be reduced very greatly-an acceptable target would be a cost between $250 and $300 per kilowatt-if the benefits of lower fuel costs are not to be offset by excessive capital charges. The reduction of capital costs is primarily a task for the engineer and the manufacturer. Major engineering development work will be required before acceptable designs and manufacturing specifications can be produced.
Canada has two power reactor projects under way, the design and construction of a demonstration power reactor, the NPD, which will have an output of 20,000 kilowatts electric, and a design study for a power reactor with an output of 200,000 kilowatts electric. Both these projects are directed toward the development of a power reactor technology based on the use of natural uranium as fuel and heavy water as moderator, the technology which Canada pioneered with the NRX reactor.

NPD, the small reactor now under construction, is a co-operative effort of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, the Canadian General Electric Company and the Hydro Electric Power Commission of Ontario. The design studies for a larger power reactor started with the work of a small group of engineers drawn from various Canadian utilities and other companies working in collaboration with A.E.C.L. staff at Chalk River.
The first report on the large reactor design study became available early in 1957. This report introduced for the first time a highly attractive design that, with development, offered excellent promise of producing power in a public utility at a cost of not more than 6 mills per kilowatt hour. In certain important respects this design was unlike that of the NPD reactor. It called for the use of horizontal pressure tubes for the containment of the pressure system including the fuel elements, in place of the single pressure vessel specified for the NPD reactor. This substitution of pressure tubes for a pressure vessel would remove one of the major problems incidental to the design and manufacture of a large nuclear power station using natural uranium as a fuel. An ingenious and very simple method of fuel loading and unloading was also proposed that almost doubles the yield of energy and therefore avoids the need of chemically processing the highly radioactive spent fuel. This was a decided improvement on the method to be used in the NPD reactor.
It was therefore decided that the work on the earlier design and on the construction of the NPD reactor should be suspended, and that a redesign should be prepared which would incorporate these new features. This redesign has been carried out by the Canadian General Electric Company in co-operation with Chalk River and the Hydro Electric Power Commission of Ontario. While the redesign has delayed the completion of this demonstration unit, now known as NPD2, it is considered that such a delay is well warranted, as it may now be considered as a prototype of a large reactor. The present design has been thoroughly evaluated, and the Chalk River staff are particularly pleased with the results and are confident that the basic design will stand comparison with any other in the world. Work has recommenced at the site near the Des Joachims power station, and the scheduled completion date of mid-1961 seems very realistic.
As I mentioned in my statement on February 1, the report of the preliminary design study for the large reactor recommended a broad program of engineering development, since such a program is essential to the


proving of the engineering feasibility of the conceptual design and the establishment of a reliable estimate of costs for a power reactor with an output of 200,000 kilowatts electric. A part of this development program will be undertaken in connection with the NPD2 reactor. However, the remainder of the proposed development work will have to be carried out independently of the NPD2 project.
It was therefore decided to establish a new division of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited in Toronto, to be known as the nuclear power plant division, which has the responsibility of directing the program for the large reactor project and co-ordinating the NPD2 project. Bearing in mind the desirability of carrying on the program in a manner which will provide for the fullest participation of the utilities and the manufacturers, the major portion of the development work will be done by contract, and it is proposed that the staff for the new division be recruited to the fullest extent possible from the utilities and manufacturers. Some manufacturers, consultants and utilities have already assigned staff to the office in Toronto. The Hydro-Electric Power Commission of Ontario is contributing 15 engineers and is making available at no cost to Atomic Energy of Canada Limited office space in Toronto for the new division.
Although the fundamental research, applied research and nuclear power programs of A.E.C.L. have been discussed separately, they may be said to have the following common objectives:
(a)	To contribute to the development of economic nuclear power in order that nuclear power may be available for use in Canada and other parts of the world where a new source of energy is required to supplement conventional sources, and to make this contribution in a manner which will provide for the most effective participation of the utilities and the manufacturers.
(b)	To expand the civil market, both domestic and foreign, for Canadian uranium.
As I stated on February 1, the net cost of A.E.C.L.'s entire program, including A.E. C.L.'s share of NPD2 and the large power reactor development program, will be $140 million spread over four years. The estimates for this fiscal year total $27.7 million. Approximately $22.7 million is for the Chalk River program, with $5 million assigned to the nuclear power plant division and NPD2.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: URANIUM CITY, SASK.    CONSTRUCTION AND ROUTE OF ACCESS ROAD
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am sure the committee will have heard with interest the statement of the minister dealing with this very important matter. Indeed, it is difficult to contemplate any question that could come before parliament which would be more

important than the question of atomic energy, which will have such a far reaching influence on our future and, indeed, may determine whether we have any future at all in this world. It is of some coincidental interest to realize that this subject has been brought up here at the beginning of the second conference at Geneva on the use of atomic energy for peaceful purposes.
Canada, as I think the minister mentioned at the beginning of his statement, has been a pioneer in the development of the use of atomic energy for peaceful purposes along with the United States and the United Kingdom. I think that over the years we have had a fine record of accomplishment in this field due largely, of course, to the skill of the scientists to whom we owe so much in the development of this new form of energy and due also in part, I think, to the backing they have been given by the Canadian government. We also owe a lot, of course, to the co-oneration we have had with the countries I have just mentioned. Our record in this field is not merely one of national progress but one of good and fruitful international co-operation.
It is interesting to recall that from the very beginning of the development of atomic energy for peaceful purposes during the war Canada, the United States and the United Kingdom have worked together in the closest kind of three-power co-operation. In those days at the beginning and right up to the time I ceased having anything to do with this matter in an official way the exchange of information was always on a three-power basis. The combined policy committee in Washington which dealt with atomic energy matters was a committee that consisted of representatives of the three countries.
I hope Canada will be able to maintain that position of equality, at least equality in regard to the exchange of information and co-operation in this field with the other two countries.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I am not really qualified in any way, shape or form to go into the scientific aspects of this matter. I confess even that there were some parts of the minister's statement that I was not able to understand as an expert would. But I did realize from his statement that in this country we are continuing to make encouraging progress in this field. I do have, perhaps, a greater understanding of the political, economic and even strategic consequences of the work that is going on. I should like for a moment to say something about the sources of atomic energy which we are fortunate enough to possess in Canada and without which we would not be able to conduct this 57071-3-286
Supply-Trade and Commerce work. I am referring, of course, to our resources of uranium which are, at the present time at least, the source of the energy in question.
I am informed that at the moment the estimated resources of uranium ore in Canada amount to 334,100,000 tons, which is 100 million tons more than that made in 1956. It is not, of course, all being developed because the uranium mining industry has grown by leaps and bounds, but the development has already begun. Uranium production in Canada in 1957 amounted to $150 million, of which we exported $127 million. In the first six months of 1958 we exported, according to the official figures, $115 million worth of uranium to the United States, which is the market for the great majority of this product, whereas in the first six months of 1957 we exported to that market only $45 million. This shows what has happened to this industry in a very short time. It is now an industry in which more than $400 million is invested in this country, and uranium will very soon be our mineral of greatest export value.
The centre of this development at the present time, the most important area, is the Blind River and Elliot Lake area. It is perhaps, at the moment, the most important uranium producing area in the world. It is a centre where, in the words of the Ottawa Journal of a few weeks ago, uranium has built a modern community, as rich and confident as any in North America.
Not long ago this government ended the government monopoly in the buying and selling of uranium, and I think that was a sensible and wise decision to make. It is now possible for uranium to be exported by producers, at least in small quantities up to 2,500 pounds, under the present regulations.
I think that was a good move to make. It is of course, as the minister will agree very necessary to keep the export of this product under control. I think the government is wise in following an arrangement which had been laid down previously, that export could only be to the countries with which we have agreements. But within the boundaries of this control, for obvious reasons which I need not go into, it is of the greatest possible importance for the development of atomic energy in Canada that we seek and find markets for this commodity abroad, and that we should not have to rely any more than is necessary-it is certainly necessary at the present time-on selling to the United States.
I realize that efforts have been made by the government in this direction, and that markets have been found in the United

Supply-Trade and Commerce Kingdom and are being sought in Japan, Switzerland and Germany. It seems to me that a very important market might be developed in Germany. I was a little disappointed to read in the Montreal Gazette a Canadian Press story dated September 1 to the effect that West Germany appears to have lost interest, at least for the present, in the purchase of Canadian uranium. The story goes on, and the minister perhaps has seen it:
Last May 21 Germany signed a contract for the purchase of Canadian uranium, and thus became the first friendly country other than Britain and the United States, to do so.
However, the contract was for the purchase of only about 15 tons of the atomic metal. It was described by government officials as a trial order, expected to be followed by a larger order for 500 tons.
Now, government officials say there have been no active negotiations for a 500-ton contract.
I hope we can press ahead with this German contract, and indeed other contracts, because as I have already said it is extremely important to diversify our market for this product, especially in view of the fact that the present contract which we have with the United States comes to an end in 1962.
There is another difficulty which is looming up in respect to the marketing of this product, which is essential for atomic energy, a difficulty which I know the minister appreciates; that is that there is now going to be increasing competition with the United States in this field. There is not now, if I can believe some of the reports I have read, the same incentive for discovery and development of uranium as there was a year or two ago, because there are indications that at the present time the supply is in excess of the demand. In that connection I was very interested to read what Dr. Lewis, who I take it is heading our delegation to the Geneva conference, had to say as reported in the press on August 31 when he arrived in Geneva. This is a United Press report. It begins:
A top atomic scientist said today the heyday of the strike it rich uranium prospector was over-at least for 15 or 20 years.
Dr. W. B. Lewis of Canada made the forecast-
He said uranium was available in such surplus that, short of discovering an excessively rich vein of the strategic metal, there were no more fortunes to be made by uranium prospecting-
"For the moment, however, the uranium prospector has had his day," Dr. Lewis added.
I would be glad if the minister could comment on that report, which undoubtedly was received with great interest by the uranium industry of this country. Some credence was given to that view in an article in the New York Times some time ago, under the heading "Uranium Plentiful, U.S. Limits Output."
[Mr. Pearson.l
An atomic energy commission spokesman said on that date, October 29, 1957, according to this report, that uranium is now so plentiful it no longer is in the interest of the government to expand production of uranium concentrate.
Then this spokesman of the United States government went on to say that continuing major explorations should be conducted. The thing that worries one is that if in fact there is enough uranium for our immediate use and if the United States authorities admit that, but at the same time are encouraging the effort in the United States for further exploration, discovery and production of uranium, this is going to be an overhanging threat to our own industry. It underlines, if it needs underlining, the desirability of the closest kind of Canada-United States co-operation not only in the field of scientific progress such as that which the minister dealt with in his statement but in the field of materials development and materials planning; the kind of planning of raw materials production which we had, in fact, during the war.
It seems to me that such planning could with advantage be applied to the production and development of this new source of energy so we shall not find ourselves in the same position as that in which we have found ourselves in this country on so many occasions in the past in connection with metals and minerals development. When there is a shortage in the United States, as there was of uranium a few years ago, they come to Canada on bended knee and ask us to do everything we can to increase production. Then they find new sources of material or metal or mineral in the United States and we are left, if I may use a colloquialism, holding the bag. I certainly hope that will not happen in the field of uranium production.
The minister referred in his statement to the United Kingdom market; and that market, of course, is of growing importance to us in this field because the United Kingdom has made, I suppose, greater progress in the development of atomic energy for power purposes, than even the United States. Under their plans there will be 12 atomic power plants in operation in the United Kingdom by 1965. That constitutes, of course, an important and growing market for our uranium.
The minister made some interesting references to the progress that has been made at Chalk River in the development of a power reactor, and the progress we have made there in this matter and in power reactor technology generally under the direction of the atomic energy board of Canada. This is an important encouraging development. One

of the encouraging features of it is that it has been a co-operative development within the country among governmental agencies like the provincial hydro commission, and private industry. The minister stated-and I do not think anyone will have any quarrel with this statement-that the government is allocating $140 million, which I think is the figure he used, spread over four years for this work. That may seem to be a large sum of money, but I feel sure that it is not too large in view of the importance of the development itself. Perhaps it does not seem so large when you relate it to the fact that it now costs about $100 million in the United States to build one atomic submarine. Perhaps as a result of this progress before long atomic power in Canada may become competitive with other sources of energy.
The Northern Miner in an edition of June 26 of this year had an extremely interesting report on this matter. In this issue of Northern Miner a statement was printed by Dr. Lewis, whom I have already quoted this morning. Dr. Lewis stated:
"We feel we have reached an objective of years of research and can now design a nuclear power plant to generate electric power at 6 mills a kilowatt hour."-
I think that was the figure the minister himself mentioned. Dr. Lewis went on to say:
But we are not stopping at just beating coal at $8 a ton-
There are some members of this house who will not get a great deal of satisfaction out of the prospect of beating coal as a source of energy, but this is Dr. Lewis' prediction:
But we are not stopping at just beating coal at $8 a ton ... We fully expect to go beyond that in power-cost cutting, which would accelerate the building of nuclear power plants not only in Canada, but in the United States and other countries.
We have always appreciated the impact the successful development of nuclear power would have on uranium-rich Canada. It would establish a broad civilian use for uranium and consequently cheap nuclear power has been a foremost objective of research at Chalk River and will likely continue to be for years to come.
The minister this morning gave us some evidence which showed that this objective certainly has not been lost sight of. But while that is a very encouraging report from one of the men in the scientific and development field and probably most concerned with this whole matter, I noticed a month or so ago a Canadian Press dispatch quoting an atomic energy engineer and scientist from an outside country. I refer to Dr. Arms of Great Britain, who said:
-electricity produced by nuclear power plants would cost 55 per cent more for construction in Canada than in Britain.

Then he went on to say this, according to this report:
He could see no reason why operating costs of a nuclear plant should be significantly different from operating costs of a conventional thermal plant in Canada. Fuel costs should not be higher in Canada than in the U.K. except for the relatively small cost of freight and insurance.
But according to his calculation that cost at the present time was a very great deal higher. If we are going to continue to progress, and if we are to realize the objective which Dr. Lewis mentioned in the statement I have read, we shall certainly have to cut down our costs of nuclear reactors.
Then there has been an interesting develop' ment in the United States in this field which I do not think the minister mentioned in his statement and which certainly has Canadian implications. That is the development-I think I have already mentioned this in the house-in the United States of what is called the Argonne low power reactor. This is a reactor which promises to be extremely important especially in Arctic territories-the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources mentioned this in his statement a few weeks ago-it is a small reactor with great power. Demountable; it weighs only ten tons, I am told. These are considerations which make it suitable as a portable power plant in remote areas. This United States portable atomic plant, according to the report I read from the United States, has been designed for Arctic operations for the reasons I have indicated, and particularly for operation in the D.E.W. line. However, this particular atomic plant is operated not by natural uranium but by enriched uranium which, I take it, in non-seientific terms is a kind of high octane uranium.
If that is the case then that would, under present conditions, give the United States a monopoly of these plants because I believe I am right in saying that we do not ourselves produce enriched uranium. I therefore ask the minister whether we could not in this country-and perhaps this is being considered; perhaps progress has been made in it-design a kind of portable atomic power plant of the type of the Argonne reactor which we could manufacture in this country as it would be designed to be operated by natural fuel. Otherwise we would be dependent on the United States for this kind of thing unless we made our own enriched fuel.
I am wondering whether we should not at this time take up with the United States in a very insistent way the question of D.E.W. line equipment of this kind, and urge that D.E.W. line or Arctic equipment to be used in Canada by the United States should be of a kind which would permit a later take

Supply-Trade and Commerce over and Canadian operation; of a kind which we could ultimately develop and manufacture in our own country. This might be of importance in the Arctic far beyond the D.E.W. line itself.
In this connection the minister of northern affairs said on August 14 in a discussion we had on northern matters, as reported at page 3513 of Hansard:
A package atomic power station developed by Atomic Energy of Canada Limited especially for such northern stations is expected to be built at the site-
He was talking about Frobisher Bay.
-although it will be coupled with diesel generated power source until day to day operation bugs are ironed out.
And then the minister is reported as having said:
We have such a station ready now but it is being run by scientists. We want to be sure it can be operated by ordinary technicians-perhaps Eskimos-before we use it as a single power source.
It would be unfortunate, I think, if we developed that single power source for Arctic use of a type suitable for us while the Americans developed the kind of power source to which I have referred for use in the north in stations to be operated by Americans a type which we could not take over and operate ourselves. I ask the minister when he replies to say something about this.
I have detained the committee for quite a considerable time, but I do not think it is necessary to apologize in view of the importance of the subject we are discussing. I shall conclude by saying that we on this side are satisfied with the minister's report, which indicates that we are making steady progress in this important field.

I hope the minister can reply to the wider issues which were raised by my leader, but in the meantime there are some other questions I should like to ask. The minister did not deal specifically in his remarks with the NRU reactor, and I wonder if he would tell us something about the temporary shut-down of that plant, whether it is to resume operation, and so on.
Next, I wonder if he would advise us of the progress being made in providing a reactor for India, which I understand is to be similar in general type to the NRX reactor. It was to have been made available under the Colombo plan, I believe, by the former government. In any event it is being continued in the program.
I would also ask the minister to tell us if there have been any changes in the personnel of the atomic energy control board as indicated in the annual report of that board for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1958, which

was tabled on June 30. The members of the board listed in that annual report were Dr. Mackenzie, president, Mr. Bateman, Mr. Bennett, Mr. Gagnon and Dr. Steacie, members of the board. I wonder, also, whether the minister would indicate any changes in the personnel of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited whose annual report was tabled on July 15 and whose officials, as of March 31, 1958 are named on the front page of that report. Perhaps I caD leave my other questions until later, when I have received a reply from the minister.

speechtext:
I am sure hon. members of the committee listened with a great deal of interest to the constructive remarks by the Leader of the Opposition, who has had considerable experience in this field in its application to affairs abroad and the implications of the use of atomic energy internationally.
I am not sure I can answer some of the questions he raised with regard to various matters and statements by various people- for example, the statement that the uranium prospector has had his day. I am not too sure about that, because while very large quantities of uranium have been discovered in various parts of the world, there are nevertheless different grades of uranium, and a prospector still has an opportunity to locate high grade ore which would, of course, be better than ore of a low grade.
I was particularly interested in the hon. gentleman's remarks about the necessity for close co-operation between the United States and Canada with respect to materiel planning. Obviously if either country overemphasizes the production of lower grade material, that would not be conducive to the long range objectives of the development of atomic energy and, moreover, we could get into difficulties with regard to overproduction. The link between Canada and the United States in the whole field of atomic energy has, of course, been quite close from the very beginning, and we keep in contact with our friends down there.
The Leader of the Opposition drew attention to a statement originating in the United Kingdom with regard to the cost of construction of atomic plants in Canada, suggesting it was unusually high compared with the United Kingdom standards. That would require examination, and I do not have the facts in front of me with regard to it at the moment. The objective is, of course, as has been stated, to arrive at lower capital costs so the target figure of 6 cents per kilowatt can be reached.
On the subject of a lower-power reactor, the Argonne, using enriched uranium, the

Leader of the Opposition made some pertinent remarks. We are interested in developing reactors that can be used in isolated areas and in the north country, but we feel that natural uranium might well be used as a fuel. Studies are being considered regarding these reactors of lesser power. The enriched uranium program followed by the United States is of course an extraordinarily expensive program. Though we are now spending millions of dollars on research and development, we cannot perhaps match all the expenditure that can be made by a country as large and as wealthy as the United States.
However, with the exchange of scientific knowledge we benefit from the things they do as they do from the things we accomplish. Whether or not they might have a monopoly with regard to this particular type of atomic plant will have to be determined later on, as experiments continue. It does not necessarily follow that an atomic reactor using enriched uranium will produce lower cost power than one with natural uranium and a heavy water coolant such as is being developed in Canada. Canada has played a prominent part in this scientific investigation.
I would like to examine some of the other matters raised in the speech of the Leader of the Opposition and perhaps convey to him later the information which is not readily at hand with regard to some of these problems as, for example, his interest in the reaction of West Germany toward contracts for uranium from Canada. I would want to examine that question and determine the state of negotiations.
The hon. member for Ottawa West asked about the NRU reactor. This went out of action on May 24 this year. That was caused by failure of one of the fuel elements where the aluminum sheath was not bonded to the uranium. As the damaged fuel element was being removed part of it fell and caught fire on top of the reactor, causing radioactive contamination to a certain extent throughout the building. But the building and equipment have been completely decontaminated, and the personnel at Chalk River with the assistance of personnel from the armed services conducted that work. There are about 160 rods to replace within the reactor and only a few of them can be removed each day, so the reactor will not be operating at its full power of 200,000 kilowatts before early October. That is the situation with regard to the NRU reactor.
The reactor for India which is being built under the Colombo plan is reaching completion and should be ready for operation in 1959. It is coming along very well. Officials of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited
Supply-Trade and Commerce have visited the plant from time to time during the last two years and have been keeping a very close eye on the work that is going on there, so perhaps a year from now that atomic plant will be in operation and will make its contribution to research and development there as our own plants are doing here in Canada.
The hon. member mentioned the atomic energy control board and the changes in personnel there. Mr. Bennett and Mr. Bateman resigned from the control board. It now consists of Doctor Mackenzie, Doctor Steacie, Doctor Gagnon, Mr. Gilchrist of Eldorado Mining and Refining Limited, now president of that firm, and Mr. Gray, the president of Atomic Energy. They comprise the board.
With regard to Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, the directors are as follows: Mr. Gray, Mr. Stewart, Mr. Duncan, Mr. Gaherty, Mr. Gordon, Mr. Hearn, Mr. O'Sullivan, Mr. Stephens, and Mr. Wallace. Resignations were received from Mr. Bennett, Mr. Ambridge, Mr. Masseu and Mr. Scully.
Before concluding my remarks on this very important topic I should like to pay my tribute to the members of the atomic energy control board and the personnel of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited for the very fine co-operation they have shown during the time I have been occupying this position. I have received nothing but the finest co-operation from them. They have relayed to me a great deal of information, and although experts in their fields and some of them very distinguished scientists they have very patiently explained the intricacies of atomic energy to a layman, and for that I am extremely grateful.
I had the opportunity last year of visiting Chalk River and seeing the plants in operation there and meeting the scientists who are doing such excellent work. I believe the program Canada embarked on some years ago and is now vigorously pursuing is really very much worth while. Canada is keeping well in the forefront of atomic energy research. We are training Canadians in this field. Their work is on a basis comparable with that of scientists in other countries. Our development work in these reactors at Chalk River and our projects for the power reactors have attracted the attention of scientists throughout the world.
It is sometimes not realized that there is a constant exchange of scientists in this nuclear field. Some of our people may be found in the United States and the United Kingdom, and representatives of those countries are here in Canada, exchanging information and learning on the spot new developments in each of these countries.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
Our people are making a distinguished contribution in the presentation of scientific papers to the meetings of learned societies dealing with the problems of nuclear physics. All told, this program has developed in Canada a body of scientists expert in the nuclear field, and as our power reactor program continues the engineering and manufacturing sides will similarly in their turn develop skilled personnel so we will be in a position to compete satisfactorily with other countries when it comes to the construction and eventually the export of machinery or the type of building that is required for an atomic reactor.
With our large supplies of uranium in Canada we want to play an active part in the supplying of uranium to countries which in time will be requiring power reactors. None of this could be done without the basic work of Canadian scientists and the application of their knowledge to reactors such as the NRU and the NRX and these power reactors which are envisaged. Then in cooperation with that application we have the very good work being done by the engineers and manufacturers, who have gained a great deal of knowledge from their activities at Chalk River. I think, by and large, we may consider that Canada is making an eminently satisfactory contribution in the field of atomic energy.

Mr. Chairman, at one o'clock I was saying that the small business community will be exceedingly disappointed with the item we are now discussing. Of course
Supply-Trade and Commerce there is nothing wrong or bad about the item itself but it is so trivial in relation to the many promises made by the government to come to the assistance of small business in this country. I have in my hand a report that appeared in the Charlottetown Guardian of February 28, 1958. It reports a speech made by the Prime Minister and reads as follows: He announced that if his government is re-elected, it is their intention at the first session of parliament to give consideration to a system whereby small business may be able to expand on reasonable terms, and have available to it a system of financing which is being considered to enable small business to meet its responsibility in expanding and assuring extra jobs. A community will continue to prosper and expand if small business expands, he said.
Where are the loans? Where is the system of credit in the item now under discussion? This is surely a very trivial and inconsequential item in comparison with the broad system of credit for small business promised by the government. The Prime Minister made speeches in many other places reiterating the same statement I have quoted from the Charlottetown Guardian. Small businessmen are very much in need of credit facilities at reasonable rates of interest. Over the years the federal government, including both Liberal and Conservative administrations has made available and continued a system of bank credits for farmers by way of guaranteed loans, guaranteed loans to fishermen and loans under the National Housing Act, but one of the very important gaps and omissions is the whole field of small business credit.
The average small businessman is not able to obtain long term credit at reasonable rates of interest. The banks cannot or do not provide credit on a long term mortgage basis. Banks will provide credit only for a short period. A businessman who needs short term credit of a few months duration to stock his store is very likely able to get that type of credit from a bank but if he needs long term credit to renovate his store or to build new premises or expand it is not readily available.
A couple of years ago we had a witness before the banking and commerce committee of the house from the hotel association of Ontario. He said that if hotel proprietors in Ontario wished to obtain money for expansion they had to pay an interest rate in excess of 14 per cent. I know of many businessmen who in order to stock their stores and provide facilities and equipment have had to go to finance companies, and borrow at rates of interest from 15 to 20 per cent per annum. The small businessman is not able to get credit in the same way a large business or corporation can. A very large incorporated business can obtain money on the money

Supply-Trade and Commerce markets. It can float debentures and obtain credit at reasonable rates. The small businessman is not able to do this. Yet in a given community it is very often the small businessman who provides credit to his customers on a short term basis without interest. He does this in competition with big business firms which are able to obtain credit for the purposes of their businesses at very low rates of interest but, when they provide credit to their customers on instalment purchases, charge interest rates of 15, 20 or 30 per cent per annum or more.
Therefore the small businessman is caught two ways. He is not able to obtain credit at reasonable rates of interest and he has to compete price-wise with big retail firms that charge enormous interest rates on instalment purchases by their customers. Because of the interest charges and the subsequent huge profits that flow to these companies therefrom they are often able to undersell the small businessman.
During this session we in the C.C.F. have made a special study of the needs of the small businessman. From time to time throughout the session members of our party have advocated measures in the interests of the small businessman. I do not know what other members are receiving in the mail but I know that I and other members of this party are receiving a great many letters from small businessmen having to do with the government's policy or lack of it as far as they are concerned. Many of these letters are identical and they are being sponsored by the retail merchants association. I have in my hand such a letter which is representative of the type of letters I have been receiving. It reads as follows:
I am writing to you in the hope that you will bring to the attention of the house the urgency of early enactment of legislation, the subject of which being small business asistance.
This subject was introduced in the throne speech and it is legislation if enacted that will redound to the benefit of the country as a whole. This is particularly true of the individual engaged in the operation of a retail store and who is desirous of obtaining terms of financing greater than that presently obtained from the chartered banks or institutions.
Small business loans can be, if patterned after the small business assistance act which our neighbours in the U.S.A. have in effect, self-liquidating . . . All that they need is government guarantee. We urge you, as our member, to voice your opinion in the house on this very important matter now.
This letter is signed by Mr. Aron Jansonn of Crestwynd, Saskatchewan. As I have said, this letter is similar to that used by a great many small businessmen in writing to their members of parliament. I would hope the minister and the government would act as

requested at an early date. We are disappointed in this estimate, which is so inadequate. We hope that action will be forthcoming in the very near future.
The small businessman is a very essential part of what is termed by many as our free enterprise economy. Most people, when they use the words "free enterprise economy", probably mean an economy wherein there are a very large number of independently owned and operated small businesses. I do not agree with the misnamed free enterprise system if by that is meant the kind of monopoly-ridden and monopoly-choked economy that we see in our country in many fields. But I do believe that the small, independent businessman, the local merchant and dealer is a very important part of our Canadian society; that he performs a very worth-while function in his community; that he is an asset to our nation, and that the government should do everything within reason to assist him to maintain the very important services that he provides.
I am one who believes very firmly in private property, so long as it is private property and so long as it is not used to exploit the community. The more private property we have, in the sense of property owned and controlled by individuals who do not use this property to try to exploit their neighbours, the better it will be for our Canadian society. We believe in private ownership, which is best illustrated by the kind of small businessman to whom I have been referring. We believe in co-operative enterprise, an association of many members in a co-operative organization on a self-help basis, with one membership to each participant and with one vote for one membership. This provides the greatest degree of democratic control of such an economic organization.
We believe in public enterprise. I referred the other day to Trans-Canada Air Lines as a publicly owned enterprise which I felt was doing an excellent service for the people of Canada. We do not feel that such a service can be provided by private enterprise, as I have defined it, by one or two people providing that service, obviously neither does it lend itself to a co-operative enterprise. We feel that rather than have Trans-Canada Air Lines owned and operated as a joint stock company or a private monopoly it is better to operate that organization under public ownership. The fourth type of ownership I would call corporate ownership, and when corporate ownership becomes a monopoly and such monopoly is used to exploit either the consumer or the worker, then we are opposed to such a type of ownership.

I feel that the government, in keeping with its election promises, should be doing far more than is being done under this legislation. There is need now for a system of credit to small business at reasonable terms of interest. I feel that is an essential step that should be taken now. Small business firms often find it very difficult to compete with the larger firms on a price basis. There is a widespread but mistaken opinion that the small, independent businessman is not efficient; that to have efficiency you have to have bigness. The reason big firms are able to override small business firms is because of their corporate strength; it is because they are able to buy more cheaply, because they can get credit more cheaply and because they are often in a position to provide credit to customers on an instalment basis at a very high rate of interest. But if the small, independent businessman in this country could have the goods laid down at his door at the same general cost level as the goods are laid down at the door of the big chain stores, I am certain that the small businessman would lick the chain stores every time. Small business can operate on a smaller margin. It can give better service, but small business has great difficulty now because of the things I have mentioned and more especially because it is unable to obtain long-term credit at reasonable rates.
I do not know why the government does not act now. I think parliament is sympathetic to the position of the small businessman. I would urge the government to fulfil its election promises, and not by providing a few thousand dollars in an estimate to hire one office manager and two or three stenographers to provide gratuitous advice to the small business people of this country. I do not think it is the kind of advice that they need. Unless the people who are appointed in accordance with this item in the estimates are most outstanding, I would question whether they are competent to give advice at all. I would be inclined to believe that the part of the item which has to do with travelling expenses is there so that the one or two officials who are appointed under this estimate may travel across the country interviewing small businessmen and learning themselves the kind of second-hand advice they should pass on if they get some letters of inquiry. I do not believe that, by this item, the government has shown that they believe at all in the free enterprise system about which they talk so much. One would wonder, from this item, whether or not the government believes at all in the system of free enterprise. However, I urge again that the government take adequate steps, even in the dying days of this session, to provide 57071-3-287
Supply-Trade and Commerce credit facilities to small, independent businessmen so that they can continue to provide essential services in their communities, and so that the government will be able to say to the Canadian public, we have kept this election promise.

I should like to take advantage of this item to bring to the minister's personal attention a matter which is of very great importance to my own constituents, indeed to all the people of Newfoundland and particularly those who have to live in the smaller settlements. My problem has to do with the regulations laid down by the division of weights and measures, in so far as they apply to the sale of coal in Newfoundland.
Prior to confederation the standard ton in Newfoundland was the British weight of 2,240 pounds. This tradition, of course, left its mark on the ways of our people. Coal is sold in most settlements in Newfoundland over the side of a ship and is unloaded into a small boat which is rowed ashore, then men shovel that coal out of the boat into a barrel or measure. Then they have to carry it sometimes as far as half a mile or a quarter of a mile up to their homes, up the land wash and overland without any roads at all. The standard measurement that has been used all this while is that of 12 tubs to the ton, which gives a tub a weight of 187 pounds. That has been an easy thing to do because they can always get a pork barrel or a beef barrel and saw it off at the required length, and that gives the exact weight and measurements for this purpose. Furthermore, this weight of 187 pounds is about the weight that two people can carry under the conditions which I have just described. Also in certain places people contribute to the schools. Instead of contributing cash they contribute a barrel of coal. I may say that the people themselves own their own measures which they take off and compare with the one on board ship. Then on shore they use that same measure with which to unload the coal from the small boat and carry it up to their storehouse. They also use that same measure to carry coal to the schoolhouse if they are contributing in kind.
The standard ton or legal ton under Canadian law is the short ton of 2,000 pounds. The division of weights and measures have laid down the regulation that the only legal measure is a tub of 100 pounds or multiples of 100 pounds. A 200 pound tub is too heavy for two people to carry around under the conditions which I have just described. Some people in Newfoundland-a very few firms, I might say-store coal for resale. The ordinary small businessman whom the hon. member for Assiniboia has just described

Supply-Trade and Commerce might carry perhaps 20 tons or 30 tons as a sort ol emergency stock to tide people over the winter it winter conditions are unusually severe. The people who stock coal in quantity use the short ton, or they have adapted themselves to the short ton, but they find it more convenient to use the 250 pound tub because two tubs weigh one-quarter ton, four tubs half a ton and eight tubs would fill up the ton. These are amounts by which coal is bought on the retail basis. I would therefore urge the minister to do one of two things. I would urge him either to suspend these regulations in so far as they apply to the resale of coal in Newfoundland or else legalize the two measurements which are most convenient for Newfoundland to use, namely the 250 pound tub and the 187 pound tub.

I will not remind the minister of the promises made during the election campaign in my riding. He promised five big bridges on the Ottawa river across from my riding to Quebec. On two occasions ministers were there in support of the Tory candidate and they were producing those promises. The Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys was one of them. However, I will not speak about politics.
I think it is a good thing that we should have some kind of credit guarantee by the government for small businessmen. I am the only one in my own town-and I thank God for it-who is able to stay in business in competition with these big companies. These big companies are using the business people in my riding to make them work for them and in ten years they will be out with nothing. It is through these big organizations or stores, through their sales, that these people are induced to buy refrigerators and everything. Many sell their products and there is nothing remaining for these people who sacrifice their own business. The point is that they do not sell on credit. It is only the small businessman who will help the people who want credit without interest. Most of the small businessmen give credit. Many of them give credit up to six months and many times-I and my friends have done it -a year without interest. If we had some kind of plan to guarantee these business people through the bank, something like that for farm development and for housing purposes, whereby a loan can be obtained at the bank at a lower interest rate, these people could give credit without interest to their customers. They treat their customers as friends, not as does big finance. Most of the time, now that a Tory government is in power, when they are short of work all over and business is bad they need more credit than ever. If it were possible to guarantee the loan to the bank or to have a special organization for small business people it would be a great advantage for all Canada. It will give credit to these people. They will buy more. As I said a moment ago, it is not for me. Up to now I have not needed a government loan. But I am only one in quite a large territory.
That would render a service to customers and give them a chance to buy the products they need-seed, agricultural machinery and so on. This is a good thing which has been promised, and this is the time to do it. As I said a minute ago the need today is greater than it was two years ago, since there is now less work and a greater shortage of money.

A measure of this sort will help to provide more work because it would give the people who need the goods a chance to buy them.
As many speakers have said, if borrowers go to the finance company they are obliged to pay interest at the rate of between 12 and 15 per cent. If, on the other hand, they bring their financial problems to the bank, the loans could be guaranteed by the federal government. The managers of the banks in the various districts are gentlemen. They know their people. They know those who should receive credit, and they know those who are likely to ask for more credit than they can handle. I do not think you could find anybody more qualified to extend credit than the managers of the banks in rural districts, certainly, and to some extent in urban areas also.
There is an urgent need for something to be done. However, I have one criticism to make. Thirty thousand dollars is not enough. It is peanuts. I myself would need more than that amount if I were to set out to buy something on any scale at all. I urge the minister, who is a businessman and who is in a position to be called the minister of business affairs, to consult with his friends in the cabinet and remind the Prime Minister of what he said so that something may be done this year to settle this urgent question.
