I judge from the opinions that have been expressed during the last half hour and just before the lunch hour that there is general agreement that a small business branch should be set up and proceed to deal with the problems of small business.
I notice from the remarks which hon. members have made that they are fully aware of the problems which affect small business and are quite sympathetic towards them. These remarks will be studied carefully and the suggestions which have been made will be given close attention. I appreciate the fact that hon. members have put on the record some of their observations gathered from their own personal experience, as the hon. member for Russell, the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo and others who are in close contact with small business and know something of the problems which small businessmen face, have indicated.
I will set out briefly the plan as we see it at the moment, and conclude with one or two comments. As has been pointed out, this arrangement was forecast in the speech from the throne in the following words:
In order to assist small business, there will be established a small business section within the administrative machinery of government. The functions of this organization will be to provide liaison between the government and small businesses, to study the problems of small business and to advise on measures necessary to meet them.
57071-3-287J
Supply-Trade and Commerce
Small business is a large and important segment of the Canadian economy in terms of its contribution to employment and national output and its worth in the life of many communities. More than four-fifths of all manufacturing establishments in the country have fewer than 50 employees and account for over one-sixth of the total selling value of factory shipments. Retail stores with under five employees represent close to nine-tenths of all establishments of this type and are responsible for over two-fifths of the total value of retail sales. In the case of wholesale trade, firms with fewer than five employees make up about two-thirds of all establishments and conduct about one-fifth of all the wholesale business in the country. Small establishments with under five employees predominate to an even greater extent in the service industries, representing almost nine-tenths of all establishments and accounting for over one-third of total receipts.
Many representations have been made to the federal government by individuals and trade associations for some form of assistance to enable small business to meet more effectively the problems with which it is confronted. Most of the proposals have involved the establishment of a service which would provide small businessmen with information and advice on their production and marketing problems.
In the light of these considerations, the main objective of the small business office would be to help small businessmen to help themselves. The following terms of reference are suggested:
1.	To act as a clearing house in referring inquiries of small business to the appropriate departments of the Canadian government or provincial and municipal governments and to various other organizations and institutions;
2.	to compile and distribute bulletins and reports on topics of general interest to small business including information on government procurement;
3.	to assist small business on request to obtain statistical, technical and other information on management, production and marketing problems;
4.	to undertake studies concerning small business, particularly for guidance of the government in developing new policies in this field and as background material for dealing more effectively with the problems of small business;
5.	in the course of its work, to consult and co-operate with educational institutions, representative business associations and other private organizations.
That, Mr. Chairman, presents in general terms the functions that will be performed by the small business office which will be set up in the Department of Trade and Commerce. The Department of Trade and Commerce has a wealth of experience in dealing with business across this country whether large or small. Within the industrial development branch of the department a great deal

Supply-Trade and Commerce of information has been compiled in the past and consequently it is appropriate that this section should be set up in this particular department where considerable experience is already available.
I appreciate the fact that some hon. members feel we have not gone far enough at this stage. That is, of course, a criticism to which any proposal is open. However, I suggest we are indicating here the government's intention to do what can be done to assist small business, and I have already indicated the importance of small business in Canada.
The paragraph in the speech from the throne and the terms of the reference which I have just read out indicate that we are aiming to determine the problems of small business before any further plans are made. I am sure hon. members will appreciate that this is the proper way to approach any subject such as this where you are entering into a relatively new field. All the facts should be assembled, representations should be heard from those engaged in small business, the operation of similar institutions in other countries should be studied and plans carefully laid for the furtherance of the interests of small business in the future.
These things cannot all be done overnight impatient as some of us may be to get on with the job. We must have this background of material before proceeding and I think this is a step in the right direction. During the course of the month of October this office will be functioning and will be available for consultation with business associations across this country and before many months have elapsed I believe there will be established a body of information from which we can draw conclusions that will be advantageous to the government in formulating its plans for the future in connection with small business.

Supply-Trade and Commerce amongst small business people during the election-and this is indicated by the actual correspondence that I receive from day to day-the minister's explanation this afternoon is going to be what I would call a damp economic squib.

It is for that reason that we believe some study should be given and an effort made to assist in a proper and sound way small industry, distribution and some services which would include tourist resorts and operations of that type.
I spoke previously at this session on this question and I do not intend to take up the time of the committee now except to say that I know dozens of small businesses which are being well operated at the present time and well managed, but because of the lack of opportunity to borrow capital over long terms at low interest they are experiencing difficulties, difficulties which are not created by inefficiency or poor management but which are created by our present economic system and by the intensive competition which comes from larger segments of our economy. I do urge that the government give consideration to every possibility of rendering the financial assistance that is so urgently needed. As this group has recommended and suggested before, it might be done through the industrial development bank; it might be done through guarantee by this government to banks of 10 per cent of the losses on loans, similar to the scheme which is provided under the Farm Improvement Loans Act, or it might de done by an amendment to the Bank Act. Mr. Chairman, may I take this opportunity on behalf of the residents of Watson and district and myself to express our gratitude to the Minister of Public Works for including in the supplementary estimates the sum of $30,000 for a new post office in Watson. This public project is long overdue and anybody who has ever seen the old post office will agree with me in what I have just said namely, that it is long overdue.
The town of Watson has a population of just over 1,000 and serves a district of approximately 20 miles in radius. Two highways go through the town of Watson and two railroads. It is a prosperous district and the people are extremely thrifty. According to the royal commission on agriculture and rural life, Watson is a town that is classified as a service centre.
To be classified as a service centre it must be a certain distance away from cities and towns. It must have facilities to give adequate service to the town and district residents. Watson can fill these requirements adequately. The closest town is located 30 miles away and the closest city about 100 miles.
Watson has a hospital, physicians, dentists, barristers, a local newspaper, theatre, bank and churches of many denominations. The town has retail facilities including clothing, household appliances, drugs, apparel and accessory stores, furniture and liquor stores. Indeed, it provides the urban and rural population with a high level of service and entertainment.
It is a fast expanding town, as just last year four gas service stations established themselves there and the Saskatchewan department of highways built a storage shed and has a service branch in this centre. All this is an indication, Mr. Chairman, that Watson is justified in obtaining a new post office to give a better service to its people.
The new post office is going to have 1,000 foot working space. Although we were desirous of 1,200 feet, nevertheless we are grateful to the minister for the proposed new building with provision to enlarge if the need arises in future.
I sincerely hope that in due course he will give consideration to other public projects in my constituency which we feel are urgently required and in many cases overdue. On behalf of Watson and district I would like the house to approve the estimates before us for a new post office in Watson, Saskatchewan.

I wish also to make one final appeal to him on behalf of the settlement of Seal Cove in Fortune bay. As I pointed out earlier, this is one of the larger fishing settlements in my riding with a population of about 500 people and a fishing population of approximately 85 or 90 fishermen. These fishermen were forced to leave the fishery years ago because the harbour had deteriorated to the point where they could not carry on the fishery successfully. Subsequently they found employment in the woods but that employment is no longer available and the people of this community are now forced to return to the fishery as the sole means of livelihood. They cannot carry on this occupation unless some dredging is done.
I have had a great deal of discussion with departmental officials concerning this question and I know it poses a dilemma for the department because the only way in which the harbour can be dredged at the present time is by hand dredging. I know we will all agree that hand dredging is not the most economical way of approaching this kind of job. On the other hand, if hand dredging is not done then the harbour cannot be made suitable for fishing for at least two or three years. This will mean the people of this settlement will have to accept able bodied relief for at least two years. There is a choice between two alternatives neither of which is very appealing. I urge the minister to take another look at this and see what can be done to make this harbour useable by the fishermen at the earliest possible date.

Mr. Chairman, although the minister's estimates were originally called as far back as June 6, I believe, today is really the first opportunity we have had to discuss in a general way the very important subject of housing in this country. It is not my intention to be in any way provocative. Instead I hope to make a straightforward examination of some of the facts that may be useful. It is not my intention to oppose what is being done but rather to urge this government to do more.
I suppose no other field has been the cause of so much mutual appreciation by
Supply-Public Works
members of the government, and perhaps that is understandable to a degree, as when they refer to their selfstyled marvellous achievements in the field of housing. The minister has himself on numerous occasions referred to the record number of housing starts, but how much of this is really due to government action? It is that aspect with which I should like to deal.
Let us now look at the facts. When parliament met on May 12 government funds had been exhausted. The Prime Minister had promised during the campaign, at which time these funds were exhausted, that more funds would be made available. Here again is another example of the government's flair for publicity which we have dealt with earlier, and I have no objection. The throne speech debate was set aside because of the so-called urgency of the situation.
The government requested and received from parliament $350 million and with the passing of this legislation much credit was taken by the government for its efforts in housing. They praised themselves for the efforts achieved by their agency lending program. Yet only a few days after this legislation was rushed through parliament the government slammed the door on agency loans and took unto themselves new authority, through Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, to enter directly into the loan field in the larger centres.
This dropping of the agency loan aspect and changing of policy caused many Canadians genuine concern. After all, people in the lower income brackets were having difficulty enough trying to arrange their financing. As I have said on earlier occasions, the lending institutions will prove to be even more selective when handling their own funds. This will cause extra hardship for the lower income borrower.
However, may I pursue the matter of the $350 million that was rushed through parliament. As I have said, only a few days later the government's policy was changed and they took the position of residual lender only. As early as June 5, Dr. Stewart Bates, president of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, had this to say on this subject:
It is anticipated by the government that this $350 million will keep us going for a year or two, and that is why we have stopped the agency arrangement at this moment of time and we are standing merely on residual loans to take care of those who cannot be picked up elsewhere. At the moment, we are leaving it to the banks and other companies to carry the program. It may be that by next September housing may be petering off in a way that the government does not like. If there has been a good demand for housing, if there are no unsold houses in December, it might be a wise policy for them to produce some more houses next winter.

Supply-Public Works
Now, my point is this. How can the government take full credit for a house building program that is being supported largely by the banks and other lending institutions? Of course, there is another version of this change in government policy. Perhaps the government is seeking more control in the field of housing. If this is true, then the government should say so. If they are seeking the use of public funds to control the number of starts made in a given period of time, then this attempt to control should be made known to the public.
Perhaps their change in policy is an attempt to hold back funds in order to assist during a future period of unemployment. I would not necessarily argue with that kind of a proposition but if this is government policy then I think they should say so.
However, regardless of the government's policies or lack of policies, the hard fact remains that the national housing legislation, desirable though it is, has been incapable of assisting 50 per cent of the Canadian people. Unfortunately, it is the 50 per cent of our Canadian wage earners who are in the medium and lower income brackets. We all recognize the splendid contribution made by the National Housing Act since its inception, but I think all will agree that it no longer does the job that was originally intended. While the top 50 per cent of the Canadian earning scale are being well looked after, the 50 per cent of our people in the lower half of the income scale are desperately in need of homes and it would seem that there is no relief in sight for them. In fact, the move is the other way. While the sizes and quality of homes grow each year to meet the popular demand from the top half, the accommodation and facilities in the lower half grow steadily worse. At this point I should like to quote very briefly from a story written by Harvey Hickey, a well-known press gallery correspondent, which appeared in the Globe and Mail and which emanated from committee meetings held in the other place. The headline reads: "Thinks All New Houses Over $20,000 Shortly", and the article goes on to say in part:
The point is rapidly being reached where it will be impossible to build a house for less than $20,000 in the Toronto area, the Senate finance committee was told today. This statement was made by L. A. Rice, president of the Toronto metropolitan home builders association-
There is a desperate need for low rental housing. As was pointed out at a recent conference of Ontario housing authorities at Niagara Falls, of the existing stock of four million dwelling units one million are over 50 years old. Half of these are in need of major repairs. It was also pointed out that one family in eight does not have private

accommodation and that many of our people are living in substandard homes.
I believe that emphasis should be placed on the low rental aspect of housing. I believe greater emphasis should be placed on the federal - provincial - municipal partnership basis, which would contribute to a greater degree to slum clearance and the rehabilitation of substandard dwellings. This is the kind of investment plan which would pay handsome dividends in the form of reduced welfare expenditures, public health, police and fire protection costs. I know the initiative for such a partnership should come from the municipalities but I would suggest that the federal authorities have a greater responsibility in bringing to the attention of the municipalities the economic benefits of such projects. With 50 per cent of our people sorely in need of better housing accommodation I suggest there is little room for complacency by the government.
We have heard several proposals in recent weeks. One was that the three levels of government, in co-operation, could acquire substandard dwellings before they fell into complete decay, rehabilitate them and lease them to those families in dire need of shelter at truly low rental figures. I would be interested to know what the government thinks of this proposition.
There is also the matter I raised in the house earlier this session, the proposition of making the financing of older homes easier. In other words, the government has been urged to take action to create a used house market as fluid as the used car market. I am wondering what the government's attitude is on this subject and if it feels this would assist families in the lower income brackets. I am sure that all of us recognize that financing of this kind is very difficult.
Many of our lower income people are forced to pay exorbitant rates of interest in an attempt to acquire even substandard accommodation. Most of us are aware of the hopeless plight of the low income borrower. He is at the mercy of every loan shark in his community, and is denied assistance through Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation because of a wage level barrier. I suggest this is not good enough for 1958, and I should like to know what the government intends to do about it.
I know it is not the responsibility of an opposition to outline policy for a government, but frankly our people are concerned about the apparent vacuum that seems to exist in so far as this government is concerned in the field of housing, and especially so soon after the election. The government must know that 50 per cent of our people are improperly housed and are unable to

improve their position through the facilities of the National Housing Act, as it is presently constituted. This is a fact. I just want to repeat that. The government knows 50 per cent of our people are improperly housed and are unable to improve their position through the facilities of the National Housing Act as it is presently constituted, yet they do very little.
I know that the government will be quick to say, but look at this new minimum house project. Well, let us look at it. If we take the minister's own words, this minimum house was designed primarily for erection in the less populated areas. While we all recognize the need for better housing in some of the more sparsely populated areas, it would seem doubtful if this minimum house will likely do much to improve the situation.
In reply to a question I put to the minister concerning Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation's attitude to this type of construction in the larger centres, the minister very properly pointed out that he doubted very much whether these homes could be built for this price in the larger centres. Therefore, it would seem evident from the minister's own statements on this subject that this minimum house project will do nothing to improve housing conditions generally, except in some rural areas.
Without being unduly critical of the government's minimum house or those who designed it, I doubt very much if its design and specifications will measure up to the desires or to the rightful ambitions of our rural population. I think it is a serious mistake for the government to assume that because people live in small communities they will be satisfied with second class accommodation. Since it is unlikely that this minimum house will meet the standards desired by our rural people and cannot, according to the minister, be built at the prices announced in urban areas, I know you will understand my hesitation at being overenthusiastic about the project at this time. However, we will be watching the acceptance of this unit in the next few months. I am sure it is the hope of all of us, and I underline this, that because of the unprecedented high cost of standard housing our people will not be forced into this minimum house construction.
Again, I do not want to be unkind or unfair, but I respectfully suggest that mass production of this minimum house, having regard for all the circumstances, could well develop into the slums of tomorrow. I would remind the minister that up to this point the corporation has a proud record of upgrading housing generally throughout Canada. While
Supply-Public Works
I do not wish to be critical of the government in this regard, I suggest that there are many other avenues open to them to ensure a steadier flow of housing in the future.
I should like to review very briefly some of these points. First, all of us are well aware of the lack of stability in the flow of mortgage funds in our respective communities. I do not believe you have any better example of this than what has transpired in the last few months. Last fall the private funds dried up and the government moved in. Then government funds were exhausted and the government promised more. The private lending institutions put money into the field. Then parliament met and more funds were approved. The government decided to cancel out their program for agency loans, and then the private institutions rushed in and since May they have been carrying the bulk of the load.
I suggest that that sort of indecision, that sort of lack of stability in providing mortgage funds in this country, does tend to have an upsetting effect. I know the government will be quick to point out the number of starts. There are many reasons to account for the number of starts. I suggest that one is the desire of all our people to have better housing, and a second is the willingness of private lending institutions, as I have shown here, to rush into the field during the last few months.
Now, I have often dealt with this subject in the house. I think it is a matter that should have most careful scrutiny by the government in order to make sure that the house construction industry can move ahead in an orderly fashion, secure in the knowledge that mortgage funds will be available. I am sure that hon. members from all parts of the house know of the reluctance of many of the lending institutions to make loans in this or that area in this or that year. Builders may well develop plans for a project, only to find the lending institutions have temporarily, and often without notice, changed their lending policies in that particular area. I sincerely believe there is a real need for a special study of this matter to ensure, as I said earlier, a steadier flow of mortgage funds for house construction.
While I am on the subject of mortgage funds, and again I do not wish to be unduly critical, may I suggest that the corporation should give consideration to finding ways and means of processing loans more expeditiously. I suppose there is not a member of this house who has not had complaints, especially from the small builders, concerning what seems to be a needlessly long delay in the cash advances to the builders. How many times have we heard them indicate their preference

Supply-Public Works
for a project that was being financed through the regular financial institutions rather than through Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation? This preference resulted from the longer waiting period apparently required by the corporation to process these advances. The need for more expeditious processing becomes more apparent if the corporation is to continue playing a major role in financing.
Another point I should like to stress at this time is that the government could lower the down payment required and in this way assist in home construction. This, of course, only adds to the carrying charges and monthly payments but it does make it easier for many of our people to take their first step.
Then, too, the government could lower the interest rate. This would be a really worthwhile contribution towards lowering the cost of houses to our people. All of us remember the frequent outbursts of the present Minister of Finance when he was on this side of the house concerning interest rates. I am not going to delay the house by reading the minister's many comments concerning the sins of high interest rates. However, I suppose the government has become so involved with its own need for borrowing that it is afraid to lower the interest rates. Here again is proof of the fact that the public, that section of the public which can least afford it, has to pay for the folly of this free-spending government.
The government could lengthen the amortization period. The average life of a home, especially with the better care it is receiving today, is much longer than the 25-year amortization period. I think we have every reason to expect an increasing life for the homes being built today. Surely, it is necessary and desirable to lengthen this amortization period. The former government, on earlier occasions, did contribute to lengthening this period to its present 25 years through amendment to the National Housing Act, and also showed real leadership in lowering the downpayment provisions below what they used to be, as well as lowering the interest rates.
Our people are also genuinely concerned about this question of increasing land costs. I realize that one of the reasons for this increase in land costs is brought about by municipalities transferring what used to be their responsibility for bringing in the trunk sewers and other services, to the land developer. These costs are now being added to the price of the land and, naturally, find their way into the mortgage. Normally, these costs would be paid on the old standard local improvement basis through the municipality. So far as the home owner is

concerned, he is not too disturbed. He pays off this additional amount over a 25-year period, rather than in the usually much shorter period under municipal financing.
However, there are many other factors that are contributing to the unusually high cost of serviced land throughout Canada, and it is to these problems that the government should be devoting their attention. Much greater use could be made of the section of the act that provides for land development on a joint co-operative basis, with the province and the municipality joining with the federal government, the latter paying 75 per cent of these costs. This legislation, where given effect, has proved very satisfactory, and I believe the government should be doing more in this field. Here again the initiative comes from the municipal or local level; but here again is an opportunity for the federal government to show leadership.
Another point I wish to make is this. The government could decrease the income requirements, thereby making the facilities of the National Housing Act legislation available to many more in the lower income categories. In this way, many of our people could make their own decision as to precisely the kind of obligations they would assume. I am sure that in the majority of cases their decision would be to buy a better home.
Mr. Chairman, there is much that could be done in the field of housing by this government. Why does it fail to act, in view of the very pressing needs of our people? Why does it choose to stand by and take credit for the house building program that is being instituted now, largely through the facilities of the lending institutions, and ignore the fact that 50 per cent of our people in the lower half of the income scale are improperly housed?
This is a time for bold and aggressive planning. This is a time for additional emphasis on research to find ways and means of, first, lowering the cost of housing and, second, making adequate housing facilities available to all of the Canadian people now in need. In its endeavours in this regard I am sure it will have the support of all hon. members in this chamber, regardless of party.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Nipissing is by nature cheerful and optimistic. I could not help feeling sorry for him as I noticed the sadness in his voice as he dealt with the housing situation in Canada today. I should hate to have him go back to North Bay in this terribly depressed frame of mind. Within the next 15 or 20 minutes I think I can make the world look infinitely better for him than it was when he rose to speak.

Whatever the faults of the government may have been, our housing policy has been one of our accomplishments of which we are extremely proud. Our only regret is that we have so little opportunity to tell the house and the Canadian people all about it. I would ask the hon. member, if he will, to think back to the situation a year ago or prior to June 10, 1957. Then he really had something about which to feel sad. Housing starts were falling off. Mortgage money was drying up. The house-building industry, which is Canada's largest, was heading for a depression. Thousands and thousands of builders across Canada would have been out of work last winter if something had not been done by the new government about this condition. Lumber mills would have been losing money and suppliers of other commodities would have been having an extremely difficult time if conditions had been allowed to continue as they were prior to June 10 of last year.
I am really surprised that the hon. member made the speech he has made today. His memory is extremely short. As everyone knows, within a few weeks of taking office the new government decided that something must be done to prevent a depression in the housebuilding industry and to help provide homes for those Canadians with modest incomes. We adopted the agency loan plan for small homes. There was available under the National Housing Act $150 million to be used on a new policy. We initiated the small homes loan plan. It was such a great success that last December we came back to the house and obtained an additional $150 million.

speechtext:
The normal source of supply had dried up before the Liberal government went out of power. They were doing absolutely nothing about the matter. We met this problem. As I pointed out, we provided an additional $150 million in December. By February that money had been going out so rapidly and houses had been started to such an extent across Canada in wintertime that we were obliged to stop loans for rental units during that month. By the time the new parliament assembled here in May practically all of the money had been used up. I have here the figures. By May $255,009,800 had been put out for small homes across Canada. Practically none of that money would have
Supply-Public Works
been spent and practically none of those homes would have been built if we had not adopted this small homes policy a year ago. It meant 26,030 units, small homes, for people with modest incomes.
We came to this new parliament during this session; one of the very first moves we made -I think it was within a week of the time the house assembled-was to bring in an amendment to the National Housing Act providing an additional $350 million in order that we could continue to encourage the construction of small homes. As of last week, $118,021,073 had been advanced. This is up to August 29. That amount was divided as follows. There was the matter of cleaning up the agency loan plan. Certain applications had been in when we ran out of money. We decided that it was only fair to enable those builders who had applied for money to get their loans from the funds that were voted in May. For that purpose $25,744,092 was advanced. That meant 2,163 additional small homes. Those are not rental units; those are small homes. In addition, for limited dividend companies which provide low rental units $21,304,281 has been advanced since May. That is infinitely more than had been advanced in a like period at any time since the National Housing Act became law. For our residual loans since May we have advanced $65,980,505. This is all since May of this year and the hon. member for Nipissing says we have been doing nothing- we have been sitting back and letting the housing situation deteriorate.
Now I am going to go to my prepared speech, Mr. Chairman. I am just a bit annoyed about the sadness with which the hon. member for Nipissing approached this problem. Before I get down to the speech which I have to read I may say that between January 1 and August 31 of this year $26,296,476 has been lent under the limited dividend schemes which is over $10 million more than was put out in the same time last year. I should also like to point out another fact which will cheer the hon. member, that loans in small centres in which he is particularly interested, from January 1 to July 31 loans have been made in respect of 14,581 units as against 7,531 units in 1957 and that in the month of July 1958 there were 1,000 more loans granted in small centres than there were in July 1957. These figures are going to be even more impressive in the future because we have a campaign going on to push these loans in the small centres, and every week these loans are increasing; by the time the hon. member gets back here next January we will be able to cheer him up even more on this particular point. And

Supply-Public Works
now to get down to this speech, because it explains what is going to happen from now on.
On May 20 of this year, by amendment to section 22 of the National Housing Act, parliament voted additional funds in an amount of $350 million for new housing through the direct lending programs of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. By the way, we were in indirect lending under our agency plan-it was our money that was going out through the offices of the banks and the lending institutions-now we are dealing direct with borrowers. The corporation was instructed to make direct residual loans on small homes to qualified applicants who are unsuccessful in obtaining loans from approved lenders. We then deliberately put ourselves in a residual position because we did not want to take over the business of providing all the mortgage money needed to build homes in Canada. This is the job of the lending institutions, and we have deliberately put ourselves into a residual position. Under the present policies, these loans are made as follows:
(a)	To prospective home owners for small homes. Refusal letters from two approved lenders must be obtained if the property is in an area having a population in excess of 55,000. One refusal letter is required in other areas.
(b)	To merchant builders for small homes, provided that the aggregate of direct loans since September, 1957 does not exceed 25 dwelling units. We put that limit on last summer that no builder could get more than 25 units, the idea being to spread the money out across the country and to as many different builders as possible and in particular to help smaller builders. The builder must obtain a refusal letter from each of two approved lenders that could normally be expected to make loans in the area. This is the plan under which the builders have been working from May until today.
(c)	To limited-dividend corporation for low rental housing. Apart from these, direct loans are not available for rental housing. We believe in these limited dividend corporation houses. That is the way to get the cheapest rents and therefore to help people with the least money. They are particularly beneficial where a service club or a church forms a limited dividend corporation for this purpose.
The statistics of these residual loans which I have given to the house from time to time indicate clearly that there is a demand for National Housing Act financing of the smaller house, and it is the smaller house in which this government is interested.

Between May 20 and August 31 of this year the corporation has made 8,302 loans for small homes in an amount of $91.7 million including the balance of agency loans. This total comprises 1,593 loans for $16.6 million to home owners in communities of
55.000	population and under; 784 loans for $8.4 million to home owners in centres of more than 55,000 population; and 5,925 loans for $66.7 million to builders in all areas. These were builders who had not previously used their quota of 25 mortgages.
In addition, from January 1 to August 31, 1958 the corporation made 33 limited-dividend loans comprising 3,325 units in an amount of $26.3 million. Of these totals, nine loans for 646 units in an amount of $5 million were approved prior to May 20. The balance, or 24 loans for 2,679 units in an amount of $21.3 million, have been made since that date.
At the same time approved lenders have almost doubled their insured lending under the act and they are expected to continue to lend at a high rate for the remainder of the year. These are the approved lenders, making regular insured N.H.A. loans. During the 35 weeks ended August 31 approved lenders made 33,285 insured loans in an amount of $391.3 million. This volume compares with 18,743 loans for $212 million in the same period last year. Almost doubled, the committee will note, and these are the loans made by the lending institutions quite apart from the small home loan plan of the government. The 1958 aggregate of all loans-insured and	direct-approved under the
National Housing Act to August 31 represents 54,916 units, which is more than double the number financed in the same period last year. Indeed, the total in 1958 to date exceeds the volume for the whole of 1957.
Taking into consideration these activities for which there is federal sponsorship or federal participation together with the normal flow of residential construction outside the National Housing Act I am convinced that total starts in 1958 will be of the order of
150.000	units. I believe that as a result of the policy I am announcing in a few minutes that might reach 160,000. Even 150,000 would constitute a record year and compares with the previous record of 138,276 starts in 1955-the highest to date-127,311 starts in 1956 and 122,340 starts in 1957. This means that there will probably be 30,000 more housing starts in 1958 than there were in 1957. That, I can assure my hon. friend, is largely due to the way in which this government has handled the housing problem. We also expect completions, as distinct from starts, to reach approximately 150,000 units which again would be a record.

Because residual loans are restricted to small, basic houses-for example, a 3-bedroom bungalow is limited to 1,050 square feet- they are making a particularly valuable contribution to families of lower incomes. This is borne out by the most recent comparison of insured loans by approved lenders and direct loans by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation for the period January 1 to June 30, 1958.
Mr. Chairman, may I have permission to have printed in Hansard a table setting out figures for the average income, cost, loan and down payment for insured and direct loans.

Canadian families with lower incomes have been enabled to obtain their own new homes and, of paramount importance, the heavy

volume of new house construction has had a tremendous impact upon the employment situation.
I do not think any Canadian will dispute that the small home policy of this government has meant thousands and thousands of jobs in the last year in Canada.
We are naturally pleased with the results. However, the government wishes to ensure that a supply of mortgage money adequate to maintain employment in the construction of small homes is available in the months ahead. The direct lending programs for homeowners and for limited dividend rental housing will, of course, continue and I am happy to inform the committee that as far as builder loans are concerned-and the merchant builders are the ones who are able to build a lot of houses quickly and that is what is needed to help create employment in the winter-an additional allotment of 25 residual loans will be made available to merchant builders, effective immediately. To be considered, completed and signed applications must be received by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation prior to December 31, 1958.
Many house builders and particularly the larger ones exhausted their allotment of 25 direct loans last winter. The government is acting to provide new quotas at this time so that builders in areas where demand is buoyant will not be delayed because of a lack of mortgage funds and will be able to proceed with another winter's operations.
The present quota of 25 to a builder will lapse. In other words, a builder who did not take advantage of the first allotment may now use only the second quota of 25. Similarly, if a builder has used ten of his original 25, he may now obtain only a total of 25, not 40. And if a builder has already used his full 25, he is still entitled only to an additional 25.
I must emphasize that this is a residual or backstop lending operation and is directed only toward the small home. I should also point out that the "minimum house" I announced to the house last week is only one type of dwelling unit that may be financed under the government's small home loan program. In other words, the financing arrangements I have been discussing today are not limited to minimum houses but may include others, provided the designs conform to the requirements already laid down as to floor area.
There are two other points. Previously, builders could qualify only if they had been engaged in house construction as merchant builders prior to September, 1957. Under the revised policy, builders may be admitted who

Supply-Public Works
operated for the first time subsequent to that time but prior to September 1, 1958.
Secondly, a builder will not receive direct loans if, at the time of application, he has more than five completed but unsold units comprising both insured and direct loans. The purpose of this restriction is, of course, to avoid direct lending to builders who have no market for their product.
Mr. Chairman, there can be no question of the impact already made by the government's actions in supplementing the flow of mortgage funds. We are equally certain that the current program, stimulated by this additional allotment of 25 loans to a builder, will ensure the construction of small homes in those areas where they are required and will, furthermore, make a vital contribution to the employment picture in Canada during the ensuing winter months.

Mr. Chairman, I have been minister for only a little over a year but my experience has been that both the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and the Department of Public Works are extremely efficient. The corporation like, I think, most other crown corporations, is set up on a business organization basis and for that reason quite a few of its practices are different from those of a department. A great deal of the publicity given in the press was sensational headline publicity and deserved to be considered as such. I have here the whole story about Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. From the peak of the staff employment in July 1956, when they had 2,369 people employed, to the end of April 1958, when they had 1,889 people employed, there had been a staff reduction amounting to 480 persons. At no time were there any mass dismissal or other such method used in reducing the staff. My memo does not say June 10, 1957 but it does say to the midsummer of 1957.
The staff reduction of 480 consisted of only 178 actual terminations owing to reductions in the establishment of various offices. This reduction of 178 took place over a period of 18 months, but the major portion was effected during the spring of 1957; for example, 118 in February 1957; 34 in April 1957; seven in March; and six in May. At the same time, during that same period, an additional 75 persons who had been hired did not complete their probationary period satisfactorily and consequently had their employment terminated. Then, there were 227 people who voluntarily resigned and were not replaced, so that the summary of the 480 works out in this way: employment terminated owing to establishment reduction, 178; employment terminated at the end of the probationary period, 75; voluntary resignations which were not replaced, 227; a total of 480.

I think the people of Canada would be interested in knowing just what amount the Canadian publications would have to pay. It would be most unfair, in my opinion, to ask the Canadian publications to pay for a deficit that is in large part due to the United States publications which are coming in and which bring absolutely no revenue to Canada.
I asked the Postmaster General, the last time I was speaking, what the increase in postal rates will be-and I am shortening my speech, Mr. Chairman, so that I will not keep you too long-or what the cost per person would be per year for having two deliveries a day instead of one delivery. I believe the Postmaster General told me that he would have these figures to submit the next time his estimates came up for consideration. Might I have an answer now, because I have other things to carry on with. I have asked this before and I thought the Postmaster General would have this ready.

Supply-Post Office

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
will be glad to accommodate the hon. member if he has somewhere else to go. He devoted a considerable portion of his remarks to our Canadian publications, and the $18 million loss which was referred to by the Auditor General in his report. I think it is correct to say that that is an estimate rather than an exact figure. I think that point should be made because of what I am going to say next, which is that our accounting and our studies of this matter do not enable us to apportion whatever loss there might be on this operation between United States and Canadian publications. We have no breakdown in that respect.
The hon. member asked about the annual cost of two deliveries a day. If we were to restrict it to five days a week, the minimum cost would be $3,750,000 a year rising ultimately to, say, $4,340,000. If it was to be done twice a day, five days a week, with one delivery on Saturday the minimum figure would be $4,800,000 rising to $5,925,000. The rise is of course due to increased payment on account of salaries and wages as employees attain more seniority. I may add that on top of that the government would also be required to supply uniforms and equipment and bear various other costs entailed in this service.

Suppose it were to cost $10 million more compared with one delivery a day. That would represent 59 cents per person per year based on a population of 17 million people. Does the minister not think that if for 59 cents we could have twice a day delivery it would not be a desirable thing to do, because in addition to providing more employment it is surely recognized that once a day mail delivery imposes a real hardship on the population which is becoming practically unbearable. I say that if for 60 cents a year we could have the benefits of twice a day delivery it would be well worth while for the post office to spend that sum. I am bringing these figures in to show what I am coming to.
The annual cost per year per person of the loan we are converting at the present time is $17 or, in the aggregate, $289,125,000 a year. Under the Liberal regime the same sum was borrowed at different times and it only cost the country $192,750,000 or $5.66 less per year per individual than is paid at the present time. If we can pay $96,375,000 more in interest under this regime than we paid for the same sum under the Liberal regime, surely we can spend 59 cents a year more per individual each year in order to get a twice a day mail delivery and have the people satisfied.

Mr. Chairman, the subject of twice a day delivery has been dealt with under the general item. I mention it only to show the minister's attitude toward mail delivery when he was an opposition member demanding twice a day service, as a preface to my opening remarks.
Some discussion took place previously with regard to postal services provided in rural areas. In the past I have urged the department to provide better rural mail services. In the majority of constituencies a large number of postal stations are served by bi-weekly or tri-weekly services and some by a once a week service. This low frequency service is out of step with the progress Canada has made in the past number of years. The situation is the same for tri-weekly service except that the waiting period is not quite as long. Why are many people living in rural areas subjected to inadequate mail services? Are they considered by the department as second class Canadians?
The minister might use the argument that the revenue does not warrant better service. This is a poor basis for argument in so far as postal services are concerned. Does the minister think that sufficient revenue is derived from postal patrons residing in street delivery areas to defray the costs of door to door delivery-I am sure he does not.
There are few, if any, postal areas that pay their own way if the costs of construction and maintenance of buildings used as post offices are taken into consideration- these costs are borne by the public works department-and also the cost of transporting mails to and from post offices by plane, train, trucks and other means of transportation.
Why do some Canadians enjoy modern, up to date mail services while other Canadians are served in the same manner, with the same degree of service as was available to our forefathers? In many rural areas the mail services have not been improved since the turn of the century.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
On
a point of order, Mr. Chairman. The hon. member has been completely off this item since he started this speech. His speech relates to the transportation branch of the department. I think, however, that the hon. member might be allowed to continue in order to save time as long as we do not get involved in a debate on that subject.

I should have said at the beginning that I intended to make a passing reference to transportation but I believe I will be saving the time of the committee by continuing my remarks at this point. I am not going to list the mail routes that serve rural

areas in the constituency of Northumberland-Miramichi on a twice a week and tri-weekly frequency, but I ask the minister to direct the attention of his officials to these areas with the end in view of improving services to daily frequency. I also request the minister to examine the scale of salaries that are paid rural postmasters because the remuneration paid in most cases is extremely low when compared with remuneration paid for the same number of duty hours in other fields either in the public service or in free enterprise.
In other departments of government parttime workers engaged for a few days each month aggregate more remuneration a year than what is paid some postmasters in rural areas who provide quarters and service six days a week for 52 weeks a year.
Charges of alleged political activities in support of the Conservative party have been made against a postmaster in Northumber-land-Miramichi, who also holds a mail contract for a side service. Every member of parliament is aware of the Postmaster General's directive issued prior to the election warning them that they would be subject to dismissal if they took part in federal politics. I do not know if there is any foundation for this charge of political activity, nor do I intend to ascertain if this mail carrier was engaged in political activity in support of the Conservative party, my reason being that I am of the opinion that a mail carrier in his hours off duty should have the right to conduct himself as he sees fit.
It should be remembered that mail contracts are awarded to the lowest bidder. That was a policy strictly followed by the former Liberal government and one which, I trust, will be continued. The time of mail drivers, other than periods during which he performs the duties under his contract, should not be regulated as to his political activities by a directive issued by a minister of the crown any more than a contractor should not be directed not to accept any other form of employment in his off-duty hours.
There may have been charges of political activity made against mail drivers in support of the Liberal party. If any charges of alleged political activity have been filed with the department the officials should make sure that charges are fully substantiated before contracts are terminated.
Mr. Chairman, shortly after March 31 of this year I received a complaint, with the assurance that a sworn affidavit would be produced if requested, that a certain postmistress was openly canvassing votes for the Conservative party. This postmistress who is alleged to have made this canvass has
Supply-Post Office
provided splendid postal services for many years and continues to do so both as a postmistress and as a conveyor of mails as a contractor for a side service. In recognition of her past services I made repeated representations to the department a few years ago for an increase in remuneration but my efforts were unsuccessful.
I did not take any action on the charge made. No attempt was made to obtain a sworn statement because I felt that this postmistress was a victim of political pressure applied by a few people whom she classed as friends who incidentally, did not reside in this postal area and did not care if she jeopardized her position as postmistress or lost her mail contract.
I was surprised when I heard about the alleged actions in view of the splendid services rendered in the past and the fact that she never engaged in political activities in former years, keeping a strictly nonpartisan attitude in keeping with her appointment as postmistress and her appointment each election year as a deputy returning officer for federal elections including the year 1958. In the best interests of the postal services and the patrons of this area I decided I would not take any action on the complaint.
The only reason these two cases of alleged political activity were brought before the committee is because the department has made a dismissal without justification for some unknown reason which appears to have a political taint. Mr. Chairman, on July 26 as found on page 2752 of Hansard of that date the member for Laurier asked the minister this question:
May I ask the minister if following this statement and because of the directive referred to have there been any dismissals from the post office?
The member for Laurier was inquiring about dismissals due to political activities on the part of mail carriers.
The minister's answer found on the same page of Hansard was:
In the case of rural mail carriers, Mr. Chairman, the answer is no.
The minister cannot make the same answer for the group of non-civil service postmasters and postmistresses. Perhaps the minister will tell the committee how many appointees in this group have been dismissed since March 31.
In the constituency of Northumberland-Miramichi the postmistress of a small revenue post office, namely, Baie Ste. Anne, has been dismissed. There are no reasonable grounds for this dismissal. On the contrary Mr. Chairman, all the known facts support the contention that the dismissal was totally unwarranted. When this postmistress took over the post office she did so after much persuasion

Supply-Post Office
by local postal patrons and on the request of area postal officials, after no other resident would accept the appointment. It was evident that this village would be without a post office if she did not accept the appointment. As a matter of fact this village was without a post office for a short period following the resignation of the former postmaster.
When this now dismissed postmistress accepted the appointment a part of her home was set aside and renovated to provide up to date service. Mail boxes and a general delivery wicket were installed at a considerable expense borne by the postmistress. The part of the home set aside for postal services was a self-contained unit and was accessible by an outside entrance used only by postal patrons. The accommodations provided were superior to the average accommodations found in most offices in rural areas. The post office was located in the centre of the community.
Since this postmistress accepted the appointment about 15 months ago the revenue of the post office tripled. District and area postal officials were completely satisfied with her performance of the duties involved. No reason was given the postmistress as to why her services were terminated. As far as she was concerned she never took the slightest part in any political activity and her services with the department were of the highest order.
The devotion to her postal duties as proven by the increases in revenue and the favourable declaration of the local postal patrons by their action in forwarding a signed petition requesting that no change be made are concrete proof of the efficient services rendered. Reliable information states that a petition signed by approximately 90 per cent of the postal patrons of this office requesting that the postmistress be retained was received by the department. The receipt of the petition is verified by the answer to my order paper No. 172. This petition was drafted and circulated by known supporters of the Conservative party and bears the signatures of a large number of supporters of the minister's own party.
It is stated that a copy of the petition was forwarded to the defeated Conservative candidate and when he was approached by a Conservative supporter, following receipt of the copy of the petition, it is alleged that the defeated candidate, who now administers both federal and provincial patronage, stated that he received the petition and that he had already recommended the dismissal of the postmistress.
Actions of this kind, Mr. Chairman, break down the morale of persons serving the public in the postal services. It places in jeopardy the appointment of non-civil service postmasters who are deemed to have cast a vote
[Mr. McWllliam.l
against this government, even though they never took the slightest part in politics.
This is the first time in my memory that a postmaster or a postmistress has been dismissed on trumped-up political reasons. It is the first time within my memory that anyone has been dismissed in the constituency of Northumberland-Miramichi for any reason other than inefficiency. In this case the people of Baie Ste. Anne are convinced that the action taken was purely of a political nature, one that had no foundation, one that was most unfair and unwarranted.
The husband of this postmistress is an active supporter of the Liberal party. He had no connection whatsoever with the post office. Surely, Mr. Chairman, a dismissal on this ground is out of keeping with our democratic system. My remarks on this dismissal have nothing to do with the newly appointed postmistress. She is a woman of splendid character and I would be the last person to criticize her or harm her good name.
This action is a new innovation in the Post Office Department and one that I would fight most strenuously if the Liberal party was in power. Non-civil service postal appointees should not be dismissed without cause, dismissed with no reason given, denied the opportunity of a right of appeal, dismissed on the recommendation of a defeated candidate of the party in power. With very few exceptions, the people of Baie Ste. Anne are indignant against the Post Office Department for such high-handed, unwarranted action meted out to one of their residents who gave splendid service and who is widely recognized as a person who never took part in politics of any kind. I feel sure the minister does not know the true facts of this case and, surely, he will have an independent investigation made, in view of the widespread protests, and if the facts are as I have presented them, then surely the course of justice will be followed and a reinstatement made. I urge, yes, Mr. Chairman, I demand that an independent survey be conducted toward bringing out the true facts surrounding this case to make sure that no injustice is done to this dismissed postmistress' good name, her character, integrity and ability.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: Just before the hon. member resumes his seat will he tell me how long this dismissed postmistress held the position?
Mr. Chairman, I know exactly just what the Postmaster General is going to say. He is going to say that this woman's appointment-

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: Answer the question.

Restrain yourself and you will get an answer. He is going to say that this woman's appointment was never made permanent, but I say that is a very flimsy excuse, Mr. Chairman. She was sworn into office the same day as the Postmaster General was sworn in; she served faithfully for over a year, tripled the service there and it is the minister's responsibility to make that appointment permanent.

Mr. Chairman, when any group of civil servants are performing a splendid job I am not only willing but very happy indeed to say something on their behalf. I want to say to the Postmaster General and through the Postmaster General to his department that not only in Niagara Falls but in the Niagara district as a whole we have some of the finest civil employees that any department could have.
As the minister well knows, Niagara Falls is the outstanding tourist section of the country and not only in the Dominion of Canada but indeed in the world. Because of that fact our mail, especially in the summer, is exceptionally heavy with respect to the postal card service. I want to say to the minister, and I think he will agree with me -if he does not he can correct me if I am wrong-that all the men in the postal department, especially the postal men themselves, have to work four hours a day on every statutory holiday with the exception of Christmas and New Years. There is an old saying that the mail has to go through regardless of the weather.
I want to pay my respects to the postal men in Niagara Falls and district. They are a fine, courteous bunch. One thing has impressed me greatly, not only in Niagara Falls but in the area. Because of the great influx of tourists you will find that the letter carriers are stopped a dozen times a day when they are on their beat and asked for directions to various parts of the city and various parts of the province. These postal men are always courteous and willing to give advice. I say to the minister that we in Niagara Falls and in the Niagara district are indeed proud of his employees and I would plead with the minister and through him to his department to give consideration to increasing the small salaries they are receiving for the fine work they are performing.

I have a very brief comment, Mr. Chairman. I have a letter from a Mrs. Leonora Starr, 129 Prospect street, Newmarket, Ontario, which contains, I think, a very interesting suggestion. Mrs. Starr has noticed that the United States postmaster is using on his cancellation stamp the words,
Business of the House
"Pray For Peace". She has made the suggestion that we in Canada should adopt the same term or a similar term. I am leaving this suggestion with the Postmaster General and I hope he will give it his kind consideration.
